abstract: Dopamine in the striatum fluctuates on fast "phasic" and slow "tonic" timescales. Although disruptions in tonic dopamine have been implicated in the pathophysiology of neuropsychiatric disease, the effect of slow, minutes-long fluctuations in dopamine on neuronal activity and behavior remain unknown. Here we use two-color fluorescence lifetime photometry at high temporal resolution (FLIPR) and calibrated optogenetic and chemogenetic manipulations to determine the impact of tonic dopamine on motivated behavior and downstream signaling in vivo. We establish a method for tracking tonic dopamine using FLIPR and determine that dopamine release fluctuates across short (100s of milliseconds) and long (10s of minutes) timescales. We find that dopamine type 1 (D1R) and type 2 (D2R) receptor expressing spiny projection neurons (SPNs) are differentially affected by changes in tonic dopamine in vivo, confirming long-standing hypothesis on tonic dopamine function in the striatum. Finally, we show that accumbal tonic dopamine levels predict and causally mediate an animal's motivation to work for reward by regulating the rate of reward-motivated actions and engagement in a progressive ratio task. Altogether, we show that tonic dopamine affects downstream signaling and motivated behavior, and establish a new set of methods that allows for careful capture and manipulation of tonic dopamine in vivo.
